examples.knowledge_point: Integrating a Quotient of Trigonometric Functions Using Trigonometric Identities
examples.worked_solution:
We can write the integral as

$$
\int_0^{\pi/3} \dfrac{\sin x}{\cos^2 x}\,\textrm d x =  \int_0^{\pi/3} \dfrac{1}{\cos x}\cdot \dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}\,\textrm d x.
$$

We then use the fact that $\dfrac{\sin x }{\cos x}  = \tan x$ and $\dfrac{1}{\cos x} = \sec x$ to express this as

$$
\int_0^{\pi/3} \sec x\tan x\,\textrm d x,
$$

which is a standard trigonometric integral. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{sec}⁡x{|}_{0}^{\pi /3} \\  & =\operatorname{sec}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})-\operatorname{sec}⁡(0) \\  & =2-1 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

We use the identity $\operatorname{cot}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\operatorname{cot}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{4}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$
